description: Component/deployment diagrams, ERDs, and the full design package.

screens.body:
Architecture is the big-boxes view of your system: which major pieces exist, what each one is responsible for, and how they talk. It answers 'what are the parts?' before anyone asks 'how does this method work?'

Good architecture makes the system explainable in five minutes and changeable without breaking everything. Bad architecture means every small change ripples everywhere.

options: The major pieces and how they talk
check.question: Architecture describes…

screens.heading: The big-boxes view

screens.body:
A component diagram shows the system's building blocks and their interfaces — the contracts they expose. A box labeled 'Payments' with an interface 'charge(card)' tells you what it offers without showing its insides.

Components connect through interfaces, not through each other's internals. That boundary is what lets two teams build two components in parallel without stepping on each other.

options: The contracts they expose to others
check.question: Component diagrams show…

screens.heading: Component diagrams
screens.keyPoint: Components connect through interfaces, not internals.

screens.body:
A deployment diagram shows where software runs: nodes are devices or servers (phone, web server, database server), and artifacts are the pieces deployed onto them (the mobile app, the API, the database).

Lines between nodes are network connections. This diagram answers ops questions: 'if the database server dies, what breaks?' Draw it before you need it at 2 AM.

options: Nodes (devices/servers) and what's deployed on them
check.question: A deployment diagram shows…

screens.heading: Deployment diagrams
screens.keyPoint: Where the software lives and what breaks if a node dies.

screens.body:
An ERD — Entity Relationship Diagram — maps your data on one page. Rectangles are entities (Customer, Order). Inside go attributes, with the primary key marked — the unique ID for each row.

Design the ERD before creating tables. It's far easier to spot a missing relationship on a diagram than in a migration that already ran.
screens.heading: ERDs: data on one page
screens.keyPoint: Entities, keys, and how rows link together.

screens.body:
Relationships have cardinality: how many of each side. One-to-many is the classic: one customer places many orders. Many-to-many needs a join table: students enroll in many courses, courses have many students.

Get cardinality wrong and the database either can't store reality or stores it twice. Read every relationship out loud both ways: 'one customer has many orders; each order belongs to one customer.'

check.question: One customer places many orders. That's…

screens.heading: Cardinality
screens.keyPoint: Read every relationship out loud, both directions.

screens.body:
Interfaces aren't just APIs — they're every boundary: the screens users see, the functions components expose, the data formats you exchange. Consistent interfaces mean consistent expectations.

Design interfaces deliberately: same naming style everywhere, same error format from every endpoint, same button patterns on every screen. Inconsistency is a tax every future developer pays.

options: Same naming, same errors, same patterns everywhere
check.question: Consistent interfaces mean…

screens.heading: Designing interfaces
screens.keyPoint: Consistency at every boundary saves future pain.

screens.body:
The design package ties it all together: the requirements it satisfies, the architecture (components + deployment), the data model (ERD), the key behaviors (sequence/activity diagrams), and the interface decisions.

Check consistency across diagrams: every entity in the ERD should trace to classes in the class diagram; every component should map to something deployed. A design where the diagrams disagree is a design that will fail in code.

options: Every diagram agrees with every other diagram
It's approved by the most people
check.question: A design package is consistent when…

screens.heading: The design package
screens.keyPoint: All diagrams must agree — that's the real review.
